rationale: B wins because it turns the weakest facts into the story instead of decorating them. Its best angle, "Substack says its top creators made over $400M last year — but won't say who or how much each," is exactly the kind of skepticism a real media-business reporter can take to an editor. A has sharper ambition, but "$400 million in creator earnings is an inconvenient number for the subscription fatigue narrative" imports a whole external discourse the update did not give it, and "YouTube runs on ads" starts a platform fight before the facts have paid for one.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief, widely published since 2022–2023" is imported context. Maybe true, maybe pitchable, but it is not in the update and the angle leans on it too hard.
"YouTube runs on ads" and the head-to-head YouTube/TikTok framing create a competitor story the supplied facts do not name. Good instinct, loose grounding.
"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack" is too confident. The update does not define whether the $400M is gross, net of Substack's cut, or limited to a cohort denominator.
"a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers" is an unnecessary invented placeholder. The creator-operator angle works without fake specificity.
gaps_in_B: "short on funding" overstates "public funding struggles." Funding trouble is supplied; current shortness is not.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" is plausible, but still an inference. The proof list catches it, but the angle headline/body state it too firmly.
"Substack takes on YouTube and TikTok with video launch" may be too quickly refused. A sourced platform-economics version could be viable; B's caution costs it one potentially strong lane.
The set underuses "over 4 million paid subscriptions" as proof of distribution scale. It cites the number, but does not build a distinct audience-scale angle around it.
